title: Apply knowledge of total quality management systems for perishable produce exportation

lessons.title: Why export fruit needs quality management
lessons.html:
The necessity of quality management

An export carton of South African fruit carries more than fruit. It carries the grower's name, the packhouse code and the reputation of the whole industry. Overseas buyers pay premium prices, but only for fruit that arrives exactly as specified: the right size, colour, sugar, firmness, packaging and label, free of pests, rot and excess residues.

If quality is left to chance, problems show up only when the container is opened in Europe or Asia. By then it is too late. The fruit may be downgraded, sold at a loss, dumped or sent back, and the exporter may face claims for the cost. Some markets also impose stricter inspection on all fruit from a country after repeated failures.

Quality management is the organised way of making sure that what the customer wants is produced every time, not just inspected at the end. It brings together:

  • the legal standards under the Agricultural Product Standards Act 119 of 1990 and PPECB requirements;
  • the market requirements of the importing country, such as phytosanitary protocols and maximum residue limits;
  • the customer specifications of retailers, which are often stricter than the legal minimum; and
  • private standards such as GLOBALG.A.P., food safety schemes and social audits like SIZA (Sustainability Initiative of South Africa).

Benefits for the farm and packhouse

  • Fewer rejections and claims, so better returns per carton.
  • Less waste of fruit, packaging and labour.
  • Clear responsibilities, so people know what to check and when.
  • Records that prove compliance to auditors and buyers.
  • Continuous learning from mistakes instead of repeating them every season.

Think of a citrus packhouse that keeps getting claims for decay on navels in the UK. Without a system, the manager blames the shipping line. With a quality management system, the team looks at fungicide records, drench concentrations, cooling times and packing dates and finds the real cause.

lessons.title: Quality control versus quality management, and a TQMS in operation
lessons.html:
Quality control (QC)

Quality control is the checking of product against a standard. In a packhouse it includes sampling cartons off the line, measuring size, colour and defects, checking weights and labels, and testing internal quality such as sugar or firmness. QC is necessary, but on its own it only finds problems after they have happened.

Quality management (QM)

Quality management is the wider system that plans, controls and improves quality. It includes QC but also asks why defects happen and how to prevent them. A total quality management system (TQMS) involves every department and every person, from orchard to dispatch, and focuses on the customer.

Quality controlQuality management
Inspects productManages the whole process
Finds defectsPrevents defects
Done by QC staffEveryone is responsible
Short term, per batchLong term, continuous improvement

The two are linked: QC results are the data that QM uses to make decisions.

Operational applications of a TQMS

  • Documented procedures for receiving fruit, drenching, grading, packing, palletising, cooling and dispatch.
  • Specifications per market and client, displayed at the packing line.
  • Critical control points for food safety, with limits, monitoring and corrective actions.
  • Training records showing that each packer and grader knows the standard.
  • Traceability using PUC (production unit code), packhouse code and pallet numbers so that any carton can be traced back to its block and packing date.
  • Supplier control for cartons, liners, labels and chemicals.
  • Non-conforming product procedures: tag, isolate, decide (repack, downgrade, local market) and record.

In practice, a line supervisor using the TQMS will stop the line when the QC sampler finds too many blemished fruit in Class 1 cartons, correct the graders and record the event, instead of letting the shift carry on and hoping the inspector misses it.

lessons.title: Validating and improving the system
lessons.html:
Validation: does the system actually work?

Having procedures on paper is not enough. Validation and verification prove that the system works in practice.

  • Validation asks whether a control is capable of achieving its purpose, for example whether the fungicide drench concentration and contact time really control decay on this fruit.
  • Verification checks that the control is being done as written, for example that the drench concentration was tested and recorded every hour.

Tools for verification

  • Internal audits by trained staff against a checklist, at planned intervals.
  • External audits by certification bodies and client audits by retailers.
  • Inspection results from PPECB export inspections: pass rates, reasons for rejection.
  • Market feedback: arrival reports, quality claims and customer complaints.
  • Records review: temperature logs, residue test results, cleaning records.

The improvement cycle: Plan, Do, Check, Act

  1. Plan: identify a problem and its cause, set a target and plan the change.
  2. Do: implement the change on a small scale or for a trial period.
  3. Check: measure results against the target.
  4. Act: if it works, make it the new standard procedure and train everyone; if not, go back to planning.

Corrective and preventive action

Every non-conformance found in an audit or a claim should get a corrective action report: what happened, the root cause, the action taken, who is responsible, the due date and how effectiveness was checked. Asking why repeatedly, sometimes called the five whys, helps reach the root cause instead of blaming the nearest person.

Management review closes the loop. At least once a season, management looks at audit results, claims, rejections and targets and decides on resources and improvements for the next season.

Key points

  • Quality management protects price, market access and reputation.
  • QC inspects product; QM manages and improves the whole process.
  • A TQMS includes procedures, specifications, training, traceability and control of non-conforming product.
  • Validation proves a control works; verification proves it is being done.
  • Plan-Do-Check-Act and corrective actions drive continuous improvement.
